page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a)); Ch 12 §8 mini-case; Tables 12-1 and 12-2; Ch 13 §3
quoted_clause: a single 8×H100 host sustains only ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s at the idealized 35%-MFU aggregate (8 × 2,472; see the Ch. 8 scope note) ... the per-GPU figure is ~2,472, not per-host
observed: The host aggregate is presented as 8 × a per-GPU rate of 2,472 tok/s, i.e. as if one 8-GPU host ran eight independent full-model replicas. But the same chapter (and Ch 13) assume the 70B is sharded across the 8 GPUs with TP=8 (140 GB of weights on 8×80 GB). Under TP=8 each GPU computes 1/8 of the FLOPs for the *shared* token stream, so each GPU sustains ~19,780 tok/s and the host aggregate is ~19,780 tok/s — the host aggregate is NOT 8× a per-GPU rate. The two printed numbers (per-GPU 2,472 and aggregate 19,776) cannot both be true under the stated layout: 2,472 = 989 TF/s × 35% ÷ 140 GFLOP/token is the rate of one GPU executing the *whole* model's FLOPs, which is impossible on one 80 GB card (140 GB of weights). The aggregate happens to be numerically right (8 × 2,472 ≈ 19,780 = the correct TP=8 aggregate) but for the wrong reason, and the printed per-GPU figure is a false statement about a single GPU's capability.
correction: Restate the prefill arithmetic as: per-GPU rate under TP=8 = 989 TF/s × 35% ÷ 17.5 GFLOP/token/GPU ≈ 19,780 tok/s; host aggregate ≈ 19,780 tok/s. If the '2,472' figure is retained, label it explicitly as a full-model-equivalent FLOP rate ('one GPU's worth of the 70B's FLOPs'), never as a per-GPU capability. Restate Candidate (c)'s throughput comparison as ≈1.25× per GPU (or 10× per host-equivalent) and adjust the surrounding prose ('throughput is genuinely much higher on the smaller model') accordingly. Reconcile with Ch 8's scope note so the two chapters use one decomposition.
acceptance_test: In Ch 12 §3, the mini-case, Tables 12-1/12-2 and Ch 13 §3, the per-GPU and host-aggregate prefill numbers satisfy: under TP=8 the host aggregate equals the per-GPU rate (each GPU contributes 1/8 of the FLOPs for the same token stream); the per-GPU rate reads 19,780 tok/s; the '2,472' figure is labelled as a full-model-equivalent FLOP rate, not a per-GPU capability; and the Candidate (c) per-GPU comparison reads ≈1.25×. A reader who asks 'could one H100 serve the 70B?' gets a consistent answer across Ch 8, Ch 12 and Ch 13.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md:19 and :79 present 2,472 tok/s as 'the per-GPU figure', but the same chapter assumes the 70B is sharded TP=8 across the host (:18 '~21 at peak', :46 'intra-host TP=8 fits the 140 GB model'); under TP=8 each GPU does 17.5 GFLOP/token, so 989e12 x 0.35 / 17.5e9 = 19,780 tok/s of stream per GPU and the host aggregate is also 19,780 - 8 x 2,472 = 19,776 matches only by cancellation. The error propagates: candidate (c)'s '24,725 prefill tok/s per H100 vs the 70B's 2,472' (:25) overstates the per-GPU advantage ~8x (true ratio 24,725/19,780 ~ 1.25x).
fix_instruction: Restate chapter-12.md:19/:79 and Table 8-1's per-GPU line so the per-GPU rate is the TP=8 share (~19,780 tok/s) and the host aggregate is the same 19,780 tok/s; if 2,472 is kept, label it a full-model-equivalent FLOP rate, not a per-GPU capability; restate candidate (c)'s comparison at :25 as ~1.25x per GPU (or ~10x per host-equivalent).

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a)) vs Ch 13 §3 'Placing the Canonical Workload' and Ch 13 §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: Ch 12: "far below the ~92K input tokens/s the workload needs on average ... a single host fails the throughput gate too"; Ch 13: "Ch11's serving analysis indicates that continuous batching + prefix caching keeps p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO on a single 8×H100 host *below capacity*"; Ch 13 mini-case: "The on-prem service is saturated: p95 TTFT has drifted to 3 s against the 2 s SLO"
observed: Ch 12 states that one host delivers ~19.8K prefill tok/s against 92K tok/s of average demand (≈21% of demand) and therefore fails the throughput gate at the canonical 10 rps average. Ch 13 states that the same single host is 'below capacity' at the canonical load, and its mini-case builds on the premise that the service was healthy at 10 rps and only became saturated after 10× traffic growth. Both cannot be true. Ch 13's further claim that 'at the 40 rps peak the queueing delay breaches it' also mischaracterizes a 18.6× aggregate capacity shortfall as a queueing-delay effect.
correction: State explicitly which notion each claim uses. If Ch 12's prefill screen stands, Ch 13's canonical placement must say the canonical workload already requires a ~6-host fleet at the 10 rps average, and the mini-case's premise must be rewritten so that the thing that saturated was the *fleet* (sized on the KV/service-time screen), not a single host. If instead Ch 11's per-host latency analysis is the intended basis, Ch 12's prefill screen must be reconciled with it (e.g., by showing that the 19.8K figure is a prefill-only ceiling that continuous batching raises, or by correcting the screen).
acceptance_test: Ch 13 §3 contains one sentence that states the canonical 10 rps average prefill demand (92K tok/s) against the per-host prefill ceiling (~19.8K) and the resulting host count (5–6), and the mini-case's premise is rewritten so that no single host is claimed to have served the canonical average load. A reader can trace the same capacity statement in Ch 12, Ch 13, Ch 16 and Ch 17 without contradiction.
verdict_evidence: chapter-13.md:44 says CB + prefix caching 'keeps p95 TTFT under the 2 s SLO on a single 8xH100 host *below capacity* - at the 40 rps peak the queueing delay breaches it', attributing single-host insufficiency to queueing/KV only, while chapter-12.md:19 and :18 show the single host is 92K / 19.8K = 4.6x short on prefill FLOPs at the 10 rps average and 368K / 19.8K = 18.6x at peak; chapter-13.md:108 then has the service healthy at 1x and saturated at 10x, with no sentence anywhere in Ch 13 naming the prefill-compute shortfall.
fix_instruction: Add the prefill-compute shortfall to chapter-13.md:44's capacity bullet: "a single host also serves only ~19.8K of the ~92K input tokens/s the 10 rps average needs (~5 hosts, Ch 12/8), so the peak failure is a compute shortfall, not merely queueing delay."

quoted_clause: §1: "Any architecture that violates any one of these is eliminated before evaluation — candidates that fail a gate are not finalists: they return to synthesis or are carried forward only as labeled sensitivity cases"; §3: "a single host fails the throughput gate too"; §6: "Candidates (a) and (b) carry forward as finalists into the evaluation chapters"
observed: Candidates (a) and (b) are defined as single-host and two-host layouts, and both fail the throughput gate as defined (19.8K ≪ 92K). §1 says such candidates 'are not carried forward as-is; it returns to synthesis for a larger layout or is dropped', yet §6 carries them forward as finalists. The reconciliation offered in §3 (replicate the host class to 5–6 hosts) changes the candidate, so the candidate carried forward is not the candidate that was evaluated. The mini-case repeats the same move: 'Candidate (a): a single 8×H100 host ... far short of the ~92K input tokens/s ... so the memory gate passes while the throughput gate already fails' — and then names (a) a finalist.
correction: Fix the gate's unit explicitly (per deployment/fleet, with per-host screens as inputs) and restate the candidates at that unit — e.g. '(a) 8×H100 host class replicated to N hosts with prefix caching' — or restate §1's elimination rule to apply to the fleet. Then make §6's finalist list consistent with the gate results as stated.
acceptance_test: §1, §3, §6, Table 12-1 and the mini-case all evaluate the same object; no candidate is described as failing a gate and simultaneously carried forward as a finalist without an explicit statement that the gate is evaluated at fleet level.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md opening: 'the payoff is a bounded set of two to three candidates, each designed to probe a distinct gate — memory fit, throughput, or quality', but the chapter's own open-gate table gives (a) 'throughput open', (b) 'throughput open at a single prefill host', (c) 'quality open' — memory fit is passed by all three (164 < 640 GB for a and b, ~15 GB for c) and two candidates probe the same gate, so the 'distinct gate' claim is not realized.
fix_instruction: Revise the opening claim to match the open-gate table, e.g. 'each designed to probe a different aspect of the constraint set — single-host throughput, phase-split throughput, or quality-vs-size (memory fit is screened for all three)', or add a fourth candidate whose binding constraint is memory fit.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a) quality paragraph); §8 mini-case; Table 12-1 open-gate table
quoted_clause: "Quality: the 70B is the workload's quality reference, so candidate (a) inherits the reference quality by definition rather than by measurement — the gate is satisfied relative to the reference, and the absolute requirement still needs the Ch 14 capability screen on the true evaluation set"; mini-case: "Quality requirements fix the model class: the system must achieve ~70B-model answer quality on enterprise prompts"; Table 12-1: "(a) | throughput open"
observed: The quality gate's threshold is expressed as a model class ('~70B-model answer quality'), which makes the gate vacuous for the 70B candidates — they satisfy it by construction — and meaningful only for the 7B candidate. §3 also concedes that (a)'s 'absolute requirement still needs the Ch 14 capability screen', i.e. (a)'s quality gate is open too, but the open-gate summary lists only 'throughput open' for (a) and 'throughput open at a single prefill host' for (b). The summary therefore understates the open gates.
correction: Express the quality requirement as an absolute threshold on the evaluation set (e.g. task accuracy / EM / rubric score ≥ X on the true eval set), so the gate can discriminate among candidates of any model class; and regenerate the open-gate table from the gate definitions so every open gate per candidate is listed.
acceptance_test: The quality gate has a metric-based threshold stated in the chapter; the open-gate table lists all open gates for (a), (b) and (c) and is consistent with §3's prose and Table 12-1's SLO column.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md Table 12-1 verdict column reads '**conditional finalist** — ✗ single-host capacity ...' for both (a) and (b), while §12.6 says 'Candidates (a) and (b) carry forward as finalists into the evaluation chapters' and §12.3 'the finalists are Candidates (a) and (b)'; §12.1 additionally states the rule 'candidates that fail a gate are not finalists', which (a) and (b) violate as single-host layouts — the book's own terminology for a candidate whose gate is still open is inconsistent across the table, §12.1, §12.3 and §12.6.
fix_instruction: Use one term for gate-open candidates throughout Chapter 12 — either 'conditional finalist' in Table 12-1, §12.3 and §12.6, or 'finalist' in the table with an explicit definition (e.g. 'finalist = advanced to evaluation, gate still open') stated next to §12.1's 'not finalists' rule.

page_hint: Ch 12 §1 (gate definition), §4 item 3, Table 12-2 'Decode pool sizing' row, §3 Candidate (b)
quoted_clause: "**throughput at the SLO** — sustained prefill and decode tokens-per-second, delivered within the latency budget (prefill + decode), must meet the workload's demand"; Table 12-2: "Decode pool sizing | none — decode shares the host (no separate pool; not sized separately) | decode pool sized to 3K tok/s avg / 12K tok/s peak | not sized in this screen"
observed: The throughput gate has two legs (prefill and decode), but only the prefill leg is screened anywhere in the chapter. The decode demand (3K tok/s average, 12K tok/s peak) is stated in §4 and in Table 12-2 but is never converted into a per-host decode rate or a host count; Table 12-2's decode row gives demand, not a count. Candidate (b)'s decode pool — the single structural difference between (a) and (b) — therefore has no size, and (b)'s cost cannot be compared with (a)'s. The chapter's own §3 also notes the decode pool 'runs bandwidth-saturated', which is precisely the quantity needed to size it.
correction: Add the decode screen: per-host decode tokens/s from the weight-read bound (140 GB of FP16 weights read per decode step ÷ per-host HBM bandwidth, times the admitted batch), then convert the 3K/12K tok/s demand into a decode-pool host count. Insert that count into Table 12-2's decode row and into Candidate (b)'s economics so (a) and (b) are costed on the same basis.
acceptance_test: Table 12-2's decode row contains a host count for (b) derived from a stated per-host decode rate; Candidate (b)'s cost statement includes the decode pool's hosts; the throughput gate is visibly evaluated on both legs.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md §12.1: '(The economic ceiling is recorded but is not one of the three gates; §12.8 states its consequence at fleet scale.)', while §12.8 concludes 'Economics is therefore recorded as *not yet passed (deferred)*' after stating 'the economic constraint, as stated, fails at fleet scale' — 'not yet passed' imports gate status onto a dimension the chapter explicitly excludes from the gate set, and conflicts with 'fails at fleet scale' in the same paragraph.
fix_instruction: Replace 'Economics is therefore recorded as *not yet passed (deferred)*' with gate-free wording such as 'Economics is therefore recorded as failing at fleet scale (the economic ceiling is not one of the three gates; it is deferred to Ch 16 and the budget renegotiation)'.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a), prefix-caching paragraph); §7 'What We Still Don't Know'
quoted_clause: "reducing effective prefill FLOPs by ~30% at 10 rps average and ~50% at peak 40 rps when many requests share common document roots"
observed: The canonical token profile is 1,200-token prompt + 8K retrieved context per request. If only the prompt is shared, the shareable prefix is 1,200/9,200 ≈ 13% of prefill FLOPs, so the 30–50% hypothesis requires substantial document-level repetition that the canonical profile does not obviously provide. The chapter labels the range [HYPOTHESIS] and flags the untested premise in §7, but never bounds the hypothesis against the canonical token profile, and the derived '~28K tokens/s' prefill figure inherits the unbounded range.
correction: State the bound explicitly in §12.3 (≤ ~13% absent document repetition; up to ~50% only if ≥ ~50% of retrieved context is shared across requests), and present the prefill-throughput effect as a range conditional on the measured prefix-hit rate rather than as a point estimate.
acceptance_test: §12.3's prefix-amortization paragraph states the maximum shareable prefix implied by the canonical token profile and conditions the 30–50% range on it; the '~28K tokens/s' figure is presented as conditional on a stated hit rate.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md §3 candidate (c): 'a 7B prefill costs only ~14 GFLOP/token, so a single card sustains ~24,700 prefill tokens/s (24,725 exact: 989 TFLOP/s × 35% MFU ÷ 14 GFLOP/token; vs ~2,472 per *GPU* for the 70B)' — the inputs are approximations the chapter itself marks with tildes ('~14 GFLOP/token', 989 is a vendor peak spec, 35% MFU is an [ASSUMPTION]), and the parallel 70B figure is written '~2,472', so 'exact' overstates precision relative to the book's own convention.
fix_instruction: Change '24,725 exact' to '~24,725 (from the stated inputs)' so it matches the tilde convention used for the 70B figure (~2,472) and does not imply more precision than 989 × 35% ÷ ~14 GFLOP/token supports.

observed: 6.24M requests at the canonical 10 rps corresponds to 624,000 s ≈ 173.3 hours of traffic per month, which equals 10 rps × 8,640 s/day × 26 days — a 24×7 basis. A business-hours basis (8 h × 22 days = 176 h) would give 6.34M requests, and the per-1K figure would be ≈$196/1K rather than $24.97/1K. The label therefore changes the reading of every per-1K number in the paragraph by ~8×, and the label as printed does not match the arithmetic of the volume.
correction: Print the derivation inline (days × hours/day × rps) next to the volume and use the matching descriptor; if the basis is 24×7, say '24×7 basis' and note the consequence for the per-1K figures.
acceptance_test: The mini-case prints the derivation of the monthly request volume and the descriptor matches it; a reader can reproduce $24.97/1K from the printed volume and cost.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md §3 candidate (b): 'with the KV hidden-state handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake)' names three systems with no source key, and chapter-12.md contains no [S#] marker, no URL and no arXiv reference anywhere (grep counts all 0), while Ch 11 §2 declares the keys book-wide ('The bracketed keys used throughout this book ... point to the primary sources below') and both Ch 11 and Ch 13 cite the same systems as '[S4][1P]' (Ch 11: 'P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake [S4][1P])'; Ch 13: 'Mooncake-style disaggregation [S4][1P]').
fix_instruction: Add the book's existing source key to Ch 12 §3: '... handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake [S4][1P])', so the named systems are traceable exactly as they are in Chapters 11 and 13.

quoted_clause: Candidate (c) does not advance as a finalist; it is carried only as a labeled sensitivity case
observed: Earlier, §12.3 says candidate (c) is 'flagged for measurement against the quality gate, not dismissed by parameter counting' and 'its fate depends on the measured quality gate.' Section 12.8 says it 'stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather than being excluded pre-measurement.' Section 12.6 then says it 'does not advance as a finalist.' These are not the same status. A candidate cannot simultaneously be excluded from the finalist set before measurement and have its finalist fate determined by a later measurement.
correction: Define a single status vocabulary. For example: 'Candidate (c) is a conditional candidate carried into the Ch 14 quality gate. If it passes, it becomes a finalist; if it fails, it is retained only as a labeled sensitivity case. It is not a finalist before that measurement.' Then make §12.6, §12.8, Table 12-1, and Fig 12.1 use that vocabulary consistently.
acceptance_test: Every mention of candidate (c)'s status in Ch 12 uses the same term and the same decision rule; a reader can state exactly what measurement promotes or rejects it.
verdict_evidence: ch12 L57 'Candidate (c) does not advance as a finalist; it is carried only as a labeled sensitivity case' — then the same paragraph says 'Candidate (c), the KV-quantized 7B model, is evaluated on the quality-degradation trade-off', L81 says it 'stays in the gate evaluation (Ch 14) rather than being excluded pre-measurement', and Table 12-1 says 'gated, not a finalist'.
fix_instruction: Adopt one status phrase everywhere — 'gated, not a finalist: carried into the Ch 14 quality gate; if it passes it becomes a finalist, otherwise it is retained only as a labeled sensitivity case' — and replace §12.6's 'carried only as a labeled sensitivity case' with it.

quoted_clause: up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget
observed: Section 12.3 defines the canonical per-host budget as 140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB. The §12.8 parenthetical gives 140 + 436 = 576 GB and calls it 'up to ~576 GB' without the ~64 GB runtime term. That is a partial sum, not the full host residency. A reader can misread 576 GB as the total residency and conclude there is 64 GB of headroom when the text elsewhere says zero headroom.
correction: Write 'up to ~576 GB of weights+KV, plus ~64 GB runtime, for ~640 GB total at the canonical per-host KV budget' or simply 'up to ~640 GB total at the canonical per-host KV budget.'
acceptance_test: The candidate (b) residency arithmetic in §12.8 sums to the same total and headroom as §12.3.
verdict_evidence: Ch12 §8 candidate (b): "up to ~576 GB (140 + 436) at the canonical per-host KV budget (§12.3)", but §12.3 states the budget as "140 GB weights + 436 GB KV + ~64 GB runtime = 640 GB — exactly the pool, zero headroom"; the parenthetical drops the 64 GB runtime term and reads as 64 GB of headroom.
fix_instruction: Make the parenthetical the full sum: "up to ~640 GB (140 weights + 436 KV + ~64 runtime) at the canonical per-host KV budget (§12.3) — zero headroom", and match Table 12-3's "~576 GB at the full KV budget (140 + 436)" cell.

quoted_clause: Total fleet cost $155.8K/mo (21 hosts) ÷ $15K = ~10.4× over the total budget
observed: "10.4× over" is ambiguous or incorrect. The cost is 10.4 times the budget; the excess over the budget is 9.4 times the budget.
correction: Use "10.4× the total budget" or "9.4× over the total budget".
acceptance_test: The ratio wording must match the arithmetic: cost/budget = 10.4, not excess/budget = 10.4.
verdict_evidence: 'Total fleet cost $155.8K/mo (21 hosts) ÷ $15K = ~10.4× over the total budget' — 155.8/15 = 10.39 is the ratio, so the excess over budget is 9.4×; the same paragraph later phrases it correctly as '~10.4× the stakeholder's stated $15,000 total monthly budget'.
fix_instruction: Change to '10.4× the total budget' (or '9.4× over') so the two sentences in the paragraph agree.

quoted_clause: ✗ ~4 avg / ~15 peak hosts at the single-H100 rate (Table 12-2)
observed: Candidate (c) is laid out as 1×H100 and Table 12-2 sizes it in "H100 cards", not 8-GPU hosts. Calling these "hosts" can be confused with the 8×H100 host unit used for Candidates (a) and (b).
correction: Change to "~4 avg / ~15 peak single-H100 cards" or "instances".
acceptance_test: All Candidate (c) capacity units should be cards/instances, not 8-GPU hosts.
verdict_evidence: Table 12-1 (c) row: '✗ ~4 avg / ~15 peak hosts at the single-H100 rate (Table 12-2)', while Table 12-2 heads the column 'Prefill capacity (hosts or cards)', gives '~4 H100 cards ... ~15 H100 cards', and its units note says '(c) is sized in single H100 cards (one card per 7B instance)'.
fix_instruction: Change Table 12-1's cell to '~4 avg / ~15 peak single-H100 cards' to match Table 12-2's units.

quoted_clause: "the KV cache is ≈15% of total residency at the canonical 9.2K context (24.1/164.1; rising past 20% beyond ~13.4K) and is often the binding constraint"
observed: The 15% figure is a per-request ratio (one request's KV over one request's weights + KV). The quantity that actually binds a host is aggregate KV across concurrent requests, which the chapter itself computes in §12.3 as 436 GB of 640 GB ≈ 68% of host memory. The bullet's own conclusion ('often the binding constraint') is not supported by the 15% number it cites, and a reader who internalizes 15% will under-weight KV in every subsequent capacity decision.
correction: Present both quantities and make the 'binding constraint' claim rest on the host-level one: per-request share (≈15% at 9.2K) and host-level share (KV budget 436 GB of 640 GB ≈ 68% at the canonical concurrency), with the context-length threshold recomputed at host level.
acceptance_test: The bullet's 'binding constraint' claim cites a host-level KV share; per-request and host-level shares are explicitly distinguished; the context-length threshold is stated for the level it applies to.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md:51 prints '24.1/164.1' (= 14.7%) and then concludes 'and is often the binding constraint', but at host level the same chapter's KV budget is 436 GB of 640 GB ~ 68% of memory (:22, :27); the 15% per-request ratio does not support the binding claim it is attached to.
fix_instruction: Rewrite chapter-12.md:51 to give both levels: 'per request the KV is ~15% of residency at 9.2K (24.1/164.1), but at the canonical host concurrency the KV budget is 436 GB of 640 GB (~68%) - which is why KV is often the binding constraint'.

quoted_clause: "adjusting the parallelism layout (e.g., parameter vs. data vs. pipeline)"
observed: 'Parameter parallelism' is not a standard term and conflicts with the book's own vocabulary (TP/PP/DP/EP, Ch 10). The intended term is tensor parallelism.
correction: Replace with 'tensor vs. data vs. pipeline (TP/DP/PP)'.
acceptance_test: The parallelism names used in Ch 12 match those used in Ch 10, Ch 12 §3 and Ch 13.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md:13 reads 'adjusting the parallelism layout (e.g., parameter vs. data vs. pipeline)'; the book's vocabulary is tensor/pipeline/data/expert (Ch 10; 'intra-host TP=8' at chapter-13.md:46), and 'parameter parallelism' is the only occurrence in the manuscript.
fix_instruction: At chapter-12.md:13 replace '(e.g., parameter vs. data vs. pipeline)' with '(e.g., tensor vs. data vs. pipeline, TP/DP/PP)'.

quoted_clause: "with the KV hidden-state handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake)"
observed: The artifact transferred between the pools is the KV cache state (K and V tensors), not 'hidden state'. 'Hidden state' is a distinct term in transformer mechanics and would mislead a reader who has just learned it.
correction: Replace with 'with the KV cache state (K/V tensors) handed between them'.
acceptance_test: The term 'hidden state' is used only for its transformer-mechanics meaning throughout Ch 12.
verdict_evidence: chapter-12.md:22 reads 'with the KV hidden-state handed between them (Splitwise / DistServe / Mooncake)'; what P/D disaggregation transfers is the KV cache (K and V tensors), which the chapter's own §4 formula at :41 defines as '2 x n_layers x n_KV-heads x d_kv x L x bytes'.
fix_instruction: At chapter-12.md:22 replace 'with the KV hidden-state handed between them' with 'with the KV cache (K/V tensors) handed between them'.

quoted_clause: "i.e. ~$232.2K self-host and ~$467.2K cloud-equivalent from the same component rates — per-host capex + energy plus a fixed ~$10K/mo staff component (Ch 16)"
observed: The cloud-equivalent at 32 hosts is exactly 32 × $14,600 = $467,200, i.e. a pure per-host figure with no staff component, whereas the self-host figure is 32 × $6,943.66 + $10,000 = $232,197. The phrase 'from the same component rates' therefore does not hold for the cloud leg, and the reader cannot tell whether the staff component is inside or outside the cloud number.
correction: State the composition of each leg explicitly (self-host = per-host capex + energy + $10K/mo staff; cloud = per-host rental only, staff excluded or included and stated), and label the $87,600 figure's basis (6 hosts at the average-load screen).
acceptance_test: Each of the three cost figures ($155,816.93, $232.2K, $467.2K) has its composition printed, and the $87,600 figure's host count is stated.
verdict_evidence: Ch12 §8 prints '~$232.2K self-host and ~$467.2K cloud-equivalent from the same component rates — per-host capex + energy plus a fixed ~$10K/mo staff component': 32×5,833.33 + 32×1,110.33 + 10,000 = $232,197.23 (Ch16 §3) but 32×730×$20 = $467,200 carries no staff term, so the 'same component rates' claim and its parenthetical hold only for the self-host leg.
fix_instruction: State each leg's composition: self-host = 32 × (capex/60 + energy) + $10K/mo staff = $232,197; cloud-equivalent = 32 × 730 h × $20 = $467,200 rental only (staff excluded, or said to be inside), and name the $87,600 = 6 × 730 × $20 basis.

quoted_clause: "All three numbers must be confirmed before a candidate is carried forward ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2))."

verdict_evidence: Ch12 §4 ends 'All three numbers must be confirmed before a candidate is carried forward ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2))' — the label trails a normative 'must be confirmed' clause, while the same chapter uses the same label on the value it actually qualifies ('The KV cache for 9.2K context at FP16 precision ([ASSUMPTION] canonical (Ch 4, Table 4-2))').
